claim: Organisms often exhibit behavioral or phenotypic diversity to improve population fitness in the face of environmental variability.
source: Organisms often exhibit behavioral or phenotypic diversity to improve population fitness in the face of environmental variability.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: When each behavior or phenotype is individually maladaptive, alternating between these losing strategies can counter-intuitively result in population persistence.
source: When each behavior or phenotype is individually maladaptive, alternating between these losing strategies can counter-intuitively result in population persistence–an outcome similar to the Parrondo's paradox.
evidence: This is the main theoretical claim of the paper, supported by the model and simulations presented.

claim: Most ecological models which exhibit paradoxical behavior depend on the presence of exogenous environmental variation.
source: Instead of the capital or history dependence that characterize traditional Parrondo games, most ecological models which exhibit such paradoxical behavior depend on the presence of exogenous environmental variation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ecological literature throughout the introduction section.

claim: The presented population model exhibits Parrondo's paradox through capital and history-dependent dynamics.
source: Here we present a population model that exhibits Parrondo's paradox through capital and history-dependent dynamics.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by mathematical modeling and numerical simulations.

claim: Even when nomadism and colonialism individually lead to extinction, switching between these strategies at the appropriate moments can paradoxically enable both population persistence and long-term growth.
source: Even when nomadism and colonialism individually lead to extinction, switching between these strategies at the appropriate moments can paradoxically enable both population persistence and long-term growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Alternating or reallocating organisms between losing strategies under certain conditions can result in meta-population persistence.
source: Counter-intuitively, even when each sub-population follows a losing strategy that will cause it to go extinct in the long-run, alternating or reallocating organisms between these losing strategies under certain conditions can result in meta-population persistence, and hence, an overall strategy that wins (Williams and Hastings, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Williams and Hastings, 2011.

claim: Random phase variation (RPV) in bacteria occurs across multiple losing phenotypes.
source: Some examples include random phase variation (RPV) in bacteria across multiple losing phenotypes (Wolf et al., 2005; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Acar et al., 2008), as well as the persistence of populations that migrate among sink habitats only (Jansen and Yoshimura, 1998; Roy et al., 2005; Benaïm and Schreiber, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Populations can persist by migrating among sink habitats only.
source: Some examples include random phase variation (RPV) in bacteria across multiple losing phenotypes (Wolf et al., 2005; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Acar et al., 2008), as well as the persistence of populations that migrate among sink habitats only (Jansen and Yoshimura, 1998; Roy et al., 2005; Benaïm and Schreiber, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Parrondo's paradox states that there are losing games of chance which can be combined to produce a winning strategy.
source: These counter-intuitive phenomena are reminiscent of Parrondo's paradox, which states that there are losing games of chance which can be combined to produce a winning strategy (Harmer and Abbott, 1999).
evidence: This is a definition of Parrondo's paradox supported by a citation.

claim: The existence of a winning combination in Parrondo's paradox relies on at least one of the losing games exhibiting either capital-dependence or history-dependence.
source: The existence of a winning combination relies on the fact that at least one of the losing Parrondo games exhibits either capital-dependence (dependence upon the current amount of capital, an ecological analog of which is population size) or history-dependence (dependence upon the past history of wins or losses, or in an ecological context, growth and decline) (Parrondo et al., 2000; Harmer and Abbott, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational Parrondo's paradox literature.

claim: Many biological studies which have drawn a connection to Parrondo games do not necessarily utilize capital-dependence or history-dependence in their models.
source: However, many biological studies which have drawn a connection to Parrondo games do not necessarily utilize capital-dependence or history-dependence in their models (Williams and Hastings, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Williams and Hastings, 2011.

claim: Models of reversal behavior in ecological settings generally rely upon the presence of exogenous environmental variation.
source: Furthermore, models of reversal behavior in ecological settings generally rely upon the presence of exogenous environmental variation (Jansen and Yoshimura, 1998; Roy et al., 2005; Benaïm and Schreiber, 2009; Wolf et al., 2005; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Acar et al., 2008; Levine and Rees, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to ecological literature.

claim: Without exogenous variation, ecological paradoxes do not occur.
source: Without exogenous variation, the paradoxes do not occur.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature about ecological models.

claim: The fitness of alleles may depend on the presence of genetic factors and epigenetic factors in previous generations.
source: The fitness of alleles may depend on the presence of genetic factors and epigenetic factors in previous generations (Reed, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reed, 2007.

claim: The fitness of any one gene can depend on the composition of other genes already present in a population.
source: More generally, the fitness of any one gene can depend on the composition of other genes already present in a population, enabling the evolution of complex adaptations like multicellularity through ratcheting mechanisms (Libby and Ratcliff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Libby and Ratcliff, 2014.

claim: Ratcheting mechanisms have recently been shown to help stabilize complex adaptations.
source: Such mechanisms have recently been shown to help stabilize these complex adaptations (Libby et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Libby et al., 2016.

claim: The storage effect can ensure that gains previously made in good years can promote persistence in less favorable times.
source: In ecological contexts, the storage effect can ensure that gains previously made in good years can promote persistence in less favorable times (Warner and Chesson, 1985; Levine and Rees, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Warner and Chesson, 1985 and Levine and Rees, 2004.

claim: Species-induced habitat destruction or resource production can have time-delayed effects on population growth, resulting in non-linear phenomena like punctuated evolution.
source: Species-induced habitat destruction or resource production can also have time-delayed effects on population growth, resulting in non-linear phenomena like punctuated evolution (Yukalov et al., 2009, Yukalov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yukalov et al., 2009 and 2014.

claim: Numerous organisms exhibit behavioral diversity analogous to nomadism and colonialism, from slime moulds and dimorphic fungi to jellyfish and human beings.
source: Numerous organisms exhibit analogous behavioral diversity, from slime moulds (amoeba vs. plasmodia) (Baldauf and Doolittle, 1997) and dimorphic fungi (yeast vs. hyphae) (Bastidas and Heitman, 2009) to jellyfish (medusae vs. polyps) (Lucas et al., 2012) and human beings.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to biological literature.

claim: The amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum is a model organism which exhibits nomadic-colonial behavior.
source: One model organism which exhibits this sort of behavior, to which our study might apply, is the amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum (Annesley and Fisher, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Annesley and Fisher, 2009.

claim: Nomads live relatively independently and are unaffected by either competition or co-operation.
source: Nomads live relatively independently, and thus are unaffected by either competition or co-operation.
evidence: This is a definition of the nomadic strategy in the model.

claim: Under poor environmental conditions, nomads are subject to steady extinction.
source: Under poor environmental conditions, they are subject to steady extinction.
evidence: This is a property of the nomadic strategy as defined in the model.

claim: Colonists live in close proximity and are subject to both competitive and co-operative effects.
source: Colonists live in close proximity, and are thus subject to both competitive and co-operative effects.
evidence: This is a definition of the colonial strategy in the model.

claim: Colonists may deplete the resources of the habitat they reside in over time, resulting in long-term death.
source: They may also deplete the resources of the habitat they reside in over time, resulting in long-term death.
evidence: This is a property of the colonial strategy as defined in the model.

claim: Organisms endowed with sensors that inform them of both population density and the state of the colonial habitat can use this information to switch from one behavior to another.
source: However, if these organisms are endowed with sensors that inform them of both population density and the state of the colonial habitat, they can use this information to switch from one behavior to another.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption of the model.

claim: An appropriate switching strategy paradoxically enables both population persistence and long-term growth.
source: Significantly, we find that an appropriate switching strategy paradoxically enables both population persistence and long-term growth – an ecological Parrondo's paradox.
evidence: This is the main finding of the paper, supported by simulation results.

claim: Competition among nomads, as well as between nomads and colonists, is taken to be insignificant due to the independence of a nomadic lifestyle.
source: Importantly, competition among nomads, as well as between nomads and colonists, is taken to be insignificant, due to the independence of a nomadic lifestyle.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: It is possible to combine nomadism and colonialism through behavioral switching such that population survival is ensured when A > 1.
source: Paradoxically, it is possible to combine these two strategies through behavioral switching such that population survival is ensured, thereby producing an overall strategy that wins.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Figure 2a is a typical example where the population becomes extinct even though it undergoes behavioral switching.
source: Figure 2a is a typical example where the population becomes extinct, even though it undergoes behavioral switching, while Figure 2b is a typical example where behavioral switching ensures population survival.
evidence: This claim refers to simulation results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Figure 2b is a typical example where behavioral switching ensures population survival.
source: Figure 2a is a typical example where the population becomes extinct, even though it undergoes behavioral switching, while Figure 2b is a typical example where behavioral switching ensures population survival.
evidence: This claim refers to simulation results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Paradoxical survival is possible because the colonial strategy is history-dependent.
source: Conceptually, this paradoxical survival is possible because the colonial strategy, or Game B, is history-dependent.
evidence: This is an analytical explanation of the mechanism behind the paradox.

claim: Switching occurs periodically, as can be seen in Figure 2b.
source: Because switching occurs periodically, as can be seen in Figure 2b, it should be noted that the organisms need not even detect the amount of resources present in the environment to implement this strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Organisms need not detect the amount of resources present in the environment to implement periodic switching; a biological clock would be sufficient.
source: Because switching occurs periodically, as can be seen in Figure 2b, it should be noted that the organisms need not even detect the amount of resources present in the environment to implement this strategy. A biological clock would be sufficient to trigger switching behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about biological implementation.

claim: Equations 10–11 are sufficient conditions for population survival.
source: Collectively, Equations 10–11 are sufficient conditions for population survival.
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical result with details in Theorems A.5 and A.6.

claim: Simulation results predict that long-term growth can occur with the optimal switching rule.
source: Simulation results predict that this can indeed occur.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The nomadic phase lasts much longer than the colonial phase, such that the amount of environmental destruction due to colonialism is limited.
source: As can be seen from Figure 3a, this is, in turn, because the nomadic phase lasts much longer than the colonial phase, such that the amount of environmental destruction due to colonialism is limited.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3a.

claim: When a large colonial population begins switching to nomadism, a significant number of colonial offspring are simultaneously being produced, resulting in more nomadic organisms than there were colonial organisms before.
source: The result is that when a large colonial population begins switching to nomadism, a significant number of colonial offspring are simultaneously being produced. These offspring also end up switching to a nomadic strategy, resulting in more nomadic organisms than there were colonial organisms before.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism behind the spikes in n₁.

claim: A particularly pronounced example of nomadic population spikes is shown in Figure 4.
source: A particularly pronounced example of this is shown in Figure 4.
evidence: This claim refers to Figure 4.

claim: The phenomenon of nomadic population spikes introduces a limiting behavior to the pattern of long-term growth.
source: However, this same phenomenon also introduces a limiting behavior to the pattern of long-term growth.
evidence: This is an analytical observation about the long-term dynamics.

claim: Significant long-term gains can be achieved via the optimal switching rule.
source: Nonetheless, it is clear that significant long-term gains can be achieved via the optimal switching rule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Limiting behavior eventually emerges in any realistic biological system.
source: Limiting behavior eventually emerges, but this is to be expected in any realistic biological system.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems.

claim: The proposed model can be easily modified for a variety of applications.
source: Our proposed model is convenient for the functional understanding of growth and survival, and can be easily modified for a variety of applications.
evidence: This is a claim about the flexibility of the model.

claim: Long-term growth is possible under both fast habitat change (Figure 7a) and slow habitat change (Figure 7b) with bounded carrying capacity.
source: As Figure 7 shows, even long-term growth is possible, under both fast habitat change (Figure 7a) and slow habitat change (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The results demonstrate the theoretical possibility of Parrondo's paradox in an ecological context.
source: The results presented in this study demonstrate the theoretical possibility of Parrondo's paradox in an ecological context.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper.

claim: Many evolutionary strategies correspond to the strategies termed as 'nomadism' and 'colonialism'.
source: Many evolutionary strategies correspond to the strategies that we have termed here as 'nomadism' and 'colonialism'.
evidence: This is a general claim about the applicability of the model.

claim: Any growth model that is devoid of competitive or collaborative effects is readily captured by Equation 2 (nomadism).
source: In particular, any growth model that is devoid of competitive or collaborative effects is readily captured by Equation 2 (nomadism), while any logistic growth model which includes both the Allee effect and habitat destruction can be described using Equations 3 and 4 (colonialism).
evidence: This is a claim about the generality of the model.

claim: Any logistic growth model which includes both the Allee effect and habitat destruction can be described using Equations 3 and 4 (colonialism).
source: In particular, any growth model that is devoid of competitive or collaborative effects is readily captured by Equation 2 (nomadism), while any logistic growth model which includes both the Allee effect and habitat destruction can be described using Equations 3 and 4 (colonialism).
evidence: This is a claim about the generality of the model.

claim: Many organisms exhibit behavioral change or phenotypic switching in response to changing environmental conditions.
source: Many organisms also exhibit behavioral change or phenotypic switching in response to changing environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems.

claim: Nomadic-colonial alternation can ensure the survival of a species, even when nomadism or colonialism alone would lead to extinction.
source: By incorporating this into our model, we have demonstrated that nomadic-colonial alternation can ensure the survival of a species, even when nomadism or colonialism alone would lead to extinction.
evidence: This is a main finding of the paper supported by simulation results.

claim: An optimal switching rule can lead to long-term population growth.
source: Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that an optimal switching rule can lead to long-term population growth.
evidence: This is a main finding of the paper supported by simulation results.

claim: The switching rules which lead to survival and long-term growth are analogous to the periodic alternation between games that produces a winning expectation in Parrondo's paradox.
source: The switching rules which lead to survival and long-term growth are analogous to the periodic alternation between games that produces a winning expectation in Parrondo's paradox.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in terms of Parrondo's paradox.

claim: The history-dependent dynamics of Game B are optimally exploited by the optimal switching rule.
source: The history-dependent dynamics of Game B are thus optimally exploited.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the optimal switching rule.

claim: The study only focuses on cases where nomadism and colonialism are individually losing strategies.
source: Firstly, the study only focuses on cases where nomadism and colonialism are individually losing strategies, despite the abundance of similar strategies that do not lose in the real world.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: If losing variants of nomadism and colonialism can be combined into a winning strategy, it follows that non-losing variants can be combined in a similar way too.
source: This is because assuming individually losing strategies in fact leads to a stronger result – if losing variants of nomadism and colonialism can be combined into a winning strategy, it follows that non-losing variants can be combined in a similar way too (see Theorem A.7 in the Appendix).
evidence: This is a logical argument about the generality of the results, supported by Theorem A.7.

claim: The population model does not encompass all variants of qualitatively similar behavior.
source: Secondly, the population model does not encompass all variants of qualitatively similar behavior.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: Many other equations can be used to model the Allee effect.
source: For example, many other equations can be used to model the Allee effect (Boukal and Berec, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boukal and Berec, 2002.

claim: The proposed model is general enough that it can be adapted for use with other equations and be expected to produce similar results.
source: Nonetheless, our proposed model is general enough that it can be adapted for use with other equations and be expected to produce similar results.
evidence: This is a claim about the robustness of the model.

claim: The presence of the Allee effect is not strictly necessary, since the colonial population might die off at low levels because of stochastic fluctuations.
source: Even the presence of the Allee effect is not strictly necessary, since the colonial population might die off at low levels because of stochastic fluctuations, rather than because of the effect.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Paradoxical behavior can occur even without the Allee effect causing long-term death of the colonial population.
source: Theorem A.7 in the Appendix also demonstrates that paradoxical behavior can occur even without the Allee effect causing long-term death of the colonial population.
evidence: This is supported by Theorem A.7 in the Appendix.

claim: It is trivially the case that pure nomadism and pure colonialism cannot out-compete a behaviorally-switching population.
source: Thirdly, though it is trivially the case that pure nomadism and pure colonialism cannot out-compete a behaviorally-switching population, a more complex analysis of the evolutionary stability of behavioral switching is beyond the scope of this paper.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the results.

claim: A more complex analysis of the evolutionary stability of behavioral switching is beyond the scope of this paper.
source: Thirdly, though it is trivially the case that pure nomadism and pure colonialism cannot out-compete a behaviorally-switching population, a more complex analysis of the evolutionary stability of behavioral switching is beyond the scope of this paper.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: Spatial dynamics are not accounted for in this study.
source: Finally, spatial dynamics are not accounted for in this study.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: Exploring spatial dynamics is a goal for future work.
source: Exploring such dynamics is a goal for future work.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Numerical simulations were performed using code written in MATLAB that relied on the ode23 ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver.
source: Numerical simulations were performed using code written in MATLAB (Source code 1) that relied on the ode23 ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: ode23 is an implementation of an explicit Runge-Kutta (2,3) pair of Bogacki and Shampine.
source: ode23 is an implementation of an explicit Runge-Kutta (2,3) pair of Bogacki and Shampine.
evidence: This is a description of the numerical method used.

claim: The accuracy of the simulation was continually checked by repeating all results with more stringent tolerance levels.
source: The accuracy of the simulation was continually checked by repeating all results with more stringent tolerance levels, ensuring that the final simulated parameters did not change significantly (by less than 1%).
evidence: This is a description of the validation methods used.

claim: Both the relative error tolerance and absolute error tolerance were determined to be 10⁻⁹.
source: Both the relative error tolerance and absolute error tolerance were determined to be 10-9.
evidence: This is a specification of the simulation parameters.

claim: The Events option of MATLAB's ODE solvers was used to detect when specific time points occurred for complex switching rules.
source: In the case of complex switching rules like Equation 13 that required modifying differential equation parameters at specific time points, the Events option of MATLAB's ODE solvers was used to detect when these points occurred.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used for complex switching rules.

claim: After each detection of a switching event, the parameters were automatically modified as per the switching rule, and the simulation continued with the new parameters.
source: After each detection, the parameters were automatically modified as per the switching rule, and the simulation continued with the new parameters.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation procedure.

claim: Broad regimes of model behavior were observed by running simulations across a wide range of parameters and initial conditions.
source: Broad regimes of model behavior were observed by running simulations across a wide range of parameters and initial conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the exploratory analysis performed.

claim: General trends and conditions observed within each regime were formalized analytically.
source: General trends and conditions observed within each regime were formalized analytically, the details of which can be found in the Appendix.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical work performed.

claim: The comprehensive model captures both capital and history-dependent dynamics within a realistic ecological setting.
source: Our comprehensive model captures both capital and history-dependent dynamics within a realistic ecological setting, thereby exhibiting Parrondo's paradox without the need for exogenous environmental influences.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model.

claim: The model exhibits Parrondo's paradox without the need for exogenous environmental influences.
source: Our comprehensive model captures both capital and history-dependent dynamics within a realistic ecological setting, thereby exhibiting Parrondo's paradox without the need for exogenous environmental influences.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the paper.

claim: The possibility of an ecological Parrondo's paradox has wide-ranging applications across the fields of ecology and population biology.
source: The possibility of an ecological Parrondo's paradox has wide-ranging applications across the fields of ecology and population biology.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the work.

claim: The ecological Parrondo's paradox could provide evolutionary insight into strategies analogous to nomadism, colonialism, and behavioral diversification.
source: Not only could it provide evolutionary insight into strategies analogous to nomadism, colonialism, and behavioral diversification, it potentially also explains why environmentally destructive species, such as Homo sapiens, can thrive and grow despite limited environmental resources.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the work.

claim: The ecological Parrondo's paradox potentially explains why environmentally destructive species, such as Homo sapiens, can thrive and grow despite limited environmental resources.
source: Not only could it provide evolutionary insight into strategies analogous to nomadism, colonialism, and behavioral diversification, it potentially also explains why environmentally destructive species, such as Homo sapiens, can thrive and grow despite limited environmental resources.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the work.

claim: The theoretical model may enable new insights into the evolution of cooperative colonies.
source: By providing a theoretical model under which such paradoxes occur, our approach may enable new insights into the evolution of cooperative colonies, as well as the conditions required for sustainable population growth.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the work.

claim: The theoretical model may enable new insights into the conditions required for sustainable population growth.
source: By providing a theoretical model under which such paradoxes occur, our approach may enable new insights into the evolution of cooperative colonies, as well as the conditions required for sustainable population growth.
